subject: BRGSA
subjectTitle: Business Research and Growth Systems Architecture

sections.rule: One correct option. Two marks each. No negative marking.
A short scenario, then a task. Both parts must be right for the marks. No partial credit.
A complete structured response. Not machine-marked.

paper.caselet: A subscription product reports that overall month-3 retention has held at 38% for a year, and the team is treating the product as stable. Split by signup month, the January cohort retained 47% at month three, April 39%, July 33% and October 28%. Monthly signups have roughly tripled over the same year.
paper.stem: What is the most defensible reading?
options: The October cohort is simply too young to judge, so the fall is an artefact of measuring groups at different ages
Signups tripling is the finding, and the retention split is a consequence of serving a larger and more varied market than before
Each new cohort is retaining worse than the one before it, and rising signup volume is holding the blended figure flat
Retention is stable, since the aggregate figure has not moved across a full year of trading and that is the measure of the product

paper.caselet: A B2B tool loses 4% of accounts a month. Exit interviews with 30 leavers find 19 never completed the initial data import, 7 left when their internal champion changed job, and 4 said a competitor was cheaper. The team is preparing a discount offer for accounts showing low usage.
paper.stem: What should the team do instead?
options: Proceed with the discount, because price is the only cause a company can act on directly and quickly
Fix the import and build a second contact inside each account, since price explains four of thirty departures
Survey the remaining accounts before acting, since thirty interviews is too small a base for any decision
Accept 4% as the market rate for this category and concentrate the effort on winning replacement accounts

paper.caselet: Seven onboarding steps each lose only a small percentage of users, but fewer than one-third reach the first value event.
paper.stem: Which principle best explains the result?
options: Reasonable step-level friction always compounds across the whole path to aha
Adding more explanatory steps will always fix the cognitive load problem
The aha moment must always be the signup event itself by definition
Small step-level losses at each stage cannot compound into anything

paper.caselet: A D2C brand validates demand with paid pre-orders. Its first cohort activates through a 21-day routine, repurchase predicts retention, and acquisition is profitable. The team now has ten experiment ideas but capacity for two.
paper.stem: Which sequence best protects the evidence chain?
options: Choose the two ideas with the highest reach scores and run them
Run all ten with smaller samples each
Optimise for the total follower count across all channels instead
Name the current constraint, score ideas against it with evidence/capacity, pre-register decisions, then reallocate after results

paper.stem: A team spends ₹3,00,000 on a channel and acquires 120 paying customers attributable to it. What is channel CAC?

paper.caselet: A team spends ₹2,00,000 on a paid channel. Their average contract value is ₹1,000 a month and their acquisition cost on that channel lands near ₹8,000.
paper.stem: What should the team do?
options: Improve the creative and the targeting first, since a high acquisition cost usually reflects a weak campaign rather than the channel.
Keep the channel and raise the price, since a contract worth more would make the same acquisition cost acceptable.
Stop the channel on price-point mismatch, because that arithmetic is settled before any creative decision is taken.
Continue for a full quarter, because paid channels need time before their true cost per customer can be judged.

paper.stem: Which order best represents the course's defensible growth chain?
options: Scale spend → validate demand → retain users → choose a metric → monetize → operate the whole system
Validate demand → run trustworthy experiments → read cohorts/economics → fix constraint → activate/retain → monetize → operate
Acquire users → count signups → add pricing tiers → survey customers → scale the spend
Build the product fully → choose a channel → define the customer → then measure the results at the end

paper.stem: Why is ‘Would you buy this?’ a weak primary validation question?
options: People cannot form a view about a product before they have seen it working in front of them
Stated intention under social pressure never reliably predicts actual purchase behaviour
Surveys always require more than a thousand responses before they mean anything
Only direct competitors are allowed to run such surveys

paper.stem: For an A/B landing-page test, which plain-language null hypothesis is best formed?
options: There is never a meaningful difference between A and B until the evidence is strong enough to reject that position
Both variants must receive an identical number of conversions before the test result can be considered valid at all
Variant B will definitely win once enough traffic has been sent through both of the pages being compared
The team prefers Variant A and should state that preference before the test begins

paper.stem: Why estimate LTV before 18 months of mature data exists?
options: To claim a precise figure for future revenue in the plan, which makes the forecast easier to defend
To replace retention measurement altogether with a single summary number that is easier to report
Because CAC never carries decision meaning without an estimate of the value it buys
Because all customers turn out to have roughly the same lifetime value anyway in practice

paper.stem: CAC is ₹12,000 and monthly gross profit per customer is ₹2,000. Ignoring churn, what is the simple payback period?
options: 6 months
10 months
24 months
4 months

paper.stem: What keeps an ICE score from becoming a polished opinion?
options: Scoring every single idea a ten on all three of the dimensions at once every time
Removing the written assumptions that sit behind each of the three scores entirely from the record
Tying all three scores to something checkable: the constraint, the evidence, and real capacity
Letting the most senior person in the room set all three of the values alone

paper.stem: A useful pricing change genuinely improves conversion, but an underpowered test concludes that nothing changed. Which error is this?
options: A Type I error, a false positive
No error because the result was not significant
Survivorship bias alone, with no testing error involved
A Type II error, a false negative

paper.caselet: Variant B leads after 18 visitors per arm. The pre-set sample target is 1,000 per arm.
paper.stem: What is the sound next action?
options: Stop the test and ship Variant B before the current lead disappears
Run the test to completion at the pre-calculated sample size
Delete Variant A from the final written report
Double-count repeat visitors so the required sample is reached sooner than the traffic allows

paper.caselet: Marketing reports four times more qualified leads than last year. Sales reports its revenue target. Customer success reports renewals. Headcount has grown and total revenue is flat.
paper.stem: What is the most defensible diagnosis?
options: Every handoff between the teams is a place the motion loses revenue that nobody records as lost.
Marketing's lead quality has fallen, which is the usual cause when volume rises and revenue does not.
One of the three teams is misreporting, since three honest reports cannot coexist with flat revenue.
The market has softened, so the same motion is producing less revenue than it did a year ago.

paper.caselet: A team reports 200 positive survey responses, 30 wait-list signups and 4 refundable deposits taken under stated terms. The founder wants to lead the investor update with the 200.
paper.stem: How should the three signals be weighted?
options: By what each cost the person to give, which makes the four deposits the primary evidence and the survey background.
By volume, since 200 responses is a far larger sample than four deposits and is therefore the more reliable number to lead with.
Equally, because each is a genuine expression of interest and discarding any of them throws away information.
By recency, taking whichever signal was collected most recently as the best guide to current demand.

paper.stem: Which pairing best fits the course's early customer-acquisition logic?
options: Both: nationwide paid acquisition at full scale from day one
B2B: focused founder-led sales; B2C: concentrated cohort launch with seeding, proof, and repurchase
B2B: mass television advertising from day one; B2C: one-to-one enterprise demonstrations
Both: wait for organic search traffic to arrive on its own

paper.stem: Why can founder-led acquisition outperform an early hired growth function?
options: Hired growth teams are not able to sell the product effectively
Founders can compress product, customer, and message learning into each conversation
Founders always cost the company far less in salary than any hired specialist would
Founder outreach automatically scales upward as the company grows larger over time

paper.stem: Which change most clearly turns cold email activity into an outbound system?
options: Sending a much larger volume of the same generic messages out to everyone every single week
Counting every single email open as a genuine sales opportunity worth adding to the pipeline
Changing the email copy every single day without ever stating a hypothesis to test first
Defining ICP, list quality, sequence and qualification as one repeatable flow, never as separate tactics

paper.stem: A low-traffic startup cannot wait for long-term revenue. Which proxy is most defensible for an onboarding experiment?
options: Whichever metric happens to move the most during the experiment window
Total page views, because it is the largest number available
Founder excitement in the weeks immediately following the launch
A faster behaviour with a documented causal link to the target outcome

paper.caselet: A founder scores building in public above community, SEO, creator seeding and a free product, then abandons it after three weeks because growth is still modest.
paper.stem: Fill both parts of the recommendation so the action and framework agree.

blanks.label: Choose the decision
options: Switch to whichever lever produced the largest case study elsewhere, because evidence from a successful company outweighs the founder's own fit score. (Zero-budget traction levers)
Choose the highest-fitting lever, write its day-30, day-60 and day-90 commitments before starting, and hold the cadence long enough for the asset to compound. (Zero-budget traction levers)
Drop the selected lever at week three and choose another, treating slow compounding as proof that the original scoring was wrong. (Zero-budget traction levers)
Run all five levers at once, since none requires paid media and the absence of budget removes the capacity trade-off between them. (Zero-budget traction levers)

blanks.label: Choose the framework
options: Zero-budget traction levers: At any moment one stage of the funnel limits the whole system, and improving any other stage moves the end-to-end outcome very little.

Zero-budget traction levers: Zero-budget traction levers compound after the work is done, but the right lever is the one whose audience, credibility and time requirements fit the founder's situation, not the one that is fashionable.

Zero-budget traction levers: Lean validation asks whether real people will take a real action on a real offer before the product is built; the build trap spends the full cost to learn the same thing afterwards.

Zero-budget traction levers: Early-stage growth is a search for repeatability run close to the founder; scale-stage growth optimises a motion already known to work, and the same move can be right at one stage and wrong at the other.

paper.caselet: A cohort retention table shows a sharp drop at days 30 to 45, immediately after a 21-day challenge ends, while a separate payment review finds failed renewals.
paper.stem: Fill both parts of the recommendation so the action and framework agree.

blanks.label: Choose the decision
options: Recover the failed payments separately, then repair what follows the 21-day programme instead of applying one general retention campaign to both forms of churn. (Voluntary versus involuntary churn)
Exclude failed payments from the analysis entirely, because involuntary churn is an operational issue that cannot be influenced by lifecycle or billing design. (Voluntary versus involuntary churn)

Combine every lost account into one churn rate and launch a discount campaign, because the same intervention should recover both dissatisfaction and failed payments. (Voluntary versus involuntary churn)
Treat the day-30 cliff as gradual dissatisfaction, since users leaving in the same month still represent a broad weakening of product value. (Voluntary versus involuntary churn)

blanks.label: Choose the framework
options: Voluntary versus involuntary churn: Voluntary versus involuntary churn separates a customer's decision from payment failure, and a cohort retention table then shows whether loss is an early drop, a stable core or a cliff tied to one event.

Voluntary versus involuntary churn: Durable retention comes from a repeatable trigger, action, variable reward and investment loop in which the user returns unprompted, not from more frequent prompting.

Voluntary versus involuntary churn: Referral mechanics include content, product, social-proof and incentivised routes; the first choice is the mechanism the product already produces naturally, not automatically paying every customer to invite someone.

Voluntary versus involuntary churn: A referral loop brings one more user; a network effect makes the product more valuable to the users already there as more relevant users join. Brand recognition, scale economies and embedded incentives are routinely mistaken for the second.

paper.caselet: A team copies a daily streak mechanic into a product customers genuinely need only during an occasional high-stakes event, and engagement rises while retention does not.
paper.stem: Fill both parts of the recommendation so the action and framework agree.

blanks.label: Choose the decision
options: Define the first recorded meeting as the AHA candidate, test whether moving users toward it improves retention, and shorten the path to that event rather than to profile completion. (Habit and lifecycle)
A substantially larger top-of-funnel for the whole team to work with each month. (Habit and lifecycle)
When retention falls, name which phase of the loop broke and repair that phase, instead of adding email or discounts. (Habit and lifecycle)
A referral discount offered to every single existing user on the mailing list. (Habit and lifecycle)

blanks.label: Choose the framework
options: Habit and lifecycle: Referral mechanics include content, product, social-proof and incentivised routes; the first choice is the mechanism the product already produces naturally, not automatically paying every customer to invite someone.
Habit and lifecycle: Durable retention comes from a repeatable trigger, action, variable reward and investment loop in which the user returns unprompted, not from more frequent prompting.

Habit and lifecycle: A referral loop brings one more user; a network effect makes the product more valuable to the users already there as more relevant users join. Brand recognition, scale economies and embedded incentives are routinely mistaken for the second.

Habit and lifecycle: Voluntary versus involuntary churn separates a customer's decision from payment failure, and a cohort retention table then shows whether loss is an early drop, a stable core or a cliff tied to one event.

paper.caselet: An underpowered test on a genuinely better pricing page reports no difference, the team keeps the old page, and the forgone gain would have compounded across every future cohort.
paper.stem: Fill both parts of the recommendation so the action and framework agree.

blanks.label: Choose the decision
options: Survivorship bias alone, with no testing error involved. (Decision errors)
Decide which of the two errors is more costly for this particular decision, then set the sample size and threshold to protect against that one. (Decision errors)
Build only the functional MVP that performs the core job, using roughly a fraction of the full effort, and keep the remaining roadmap contingent on what that build teaches. (Decision errors)
No error because the result was not significant. (Decision errors)

blanks.label: Choose the framework
options: Decision errors: A/B testing earns statistical significance only after the planned sample is reached, using the baseline, minimum detectable effect and alpha fixed before either variant's result is visible.
Decision errors: An experiment starts from the null position that nothing changed, and the variant earns the decision only when evidence collected to a pre-set sample is strong enough to reject it.
Decision errors: A Type I error scales something that does not work; a Type II error abandons something that does. Every test outcome lands in one of the four cells of that matrix.

Decision errors: Test modes follow the stakes: an expensive wrong decision needs a valid test run to its sample, while a low-stakes choice may use a directional test that is reported as suggestive rather than conclusive.

paper.caselet: A marketplace connecting small firms with freelance designers reports 46,000 monthly visitors, up from 19,000 a year ago. Of those visitors, 5,980 register, 1,140 post a first brief, and 391 complete a first hire. The team's own benchmarks put visitor-to-registration at 12%, registration-to-brief at 55% and brief-to-hire at 35%. Two channels supply the traffic. Paid search costs ₹2,700 per registration and those users complete a first hire 4% of the time; designers inviting their own existing clients costs nothing and those users complete a first hire 31% of the time, but the invitation flow is buried three screens inside the designer dashboard and 6% of designers have ever used it. The quarterly plan allocates 80% of the budget to paid search on the grounds that it is the larger source of registrations. The company's weekly dashboard shows visitors, registrations and gross merchandise value; no line has an owner, a threshold, or a stated action if it moves.
paper.stem: Write the case you would put to this team before the quarterly budget is committed. Say where the money should go and why, and be specific about which number is the one that matters.

paper.caselet: A grocery-delivery app works in one city, where 34% of users order weekly and unprompted word of mouth supplies 61% of new users at no acquisition cost. It launched in four more cities on the strength of that. In the new cities, 7% order weekly, word of mouth supplies 9%, and acquisition runs at ₹740 per user through discount vouchers. The single operational difference is delivery time: 24 minutes in the original city against 71 minutes in the others, where the app has no dark store and picks from partner supermarkets. A test of a daily-streak reward, modelled on a language-learning app, ran across the new cities for five weeks and showed no effect; the sample was 600 users per arm against a required 7,000, and the feature has been abandoned. Nobody has tested reducing delivery time. Groceries are bought about once a week by these users, and the original city's ordering pattern is concentrated on Saturday mornings. The team is proposing to raise voucher spend in the four cities to buy the word-of-mouth flywheel it saw at home.
paper.stem: Write the assessment of this expansion. Address the voucher proposal and the abandoned streak feature, and say what should be tested next.
